**Ch 011 draft — paragraph beginning "The last time Henry Adams saw Thackeray…"**

Source: "was in entering the house of Sir Henry Holland for an evening reception. Thackeray was pulling on his coat downstairs, laughing because, in his usual blind way, he had stumbled into the wrong house…"

Draft: "was in entering a house for an evening reception. Thackeray, laughing at having blundered into the wrong door, suddenly spoke of his—and Adams's—friend, Mrs. Frank Hampton…"

Sir Henry Holland is an authorized removal. The vague "a house" is fine. No structural damage here — a competent reader understands the anecdote without needing the host's name.

---

**Ch 011 draft — "Ten years afterwards he bubbled with delight at a call on Hugo"**

Source: "Ten years afterwards Adams met him at the Geneva Conference, fresh from Paris, bubbling with delight at a call he had made on Hugo: 'I was shown into a large room,' he said…"

Draft: "Ten years afterwards he bubbled with delight at a call on Hugo: 'I was shown into a large room,' he said…"

The pronoun "he" — what is its antecedent in the draft? The preceding sentences in the draft are: "Even Milnes, who felt the splendors of Hugo and Landor, was almost as helpless in personal contact with them. Ten years afterwards he bubbled with delight at a call on Hugo: 'I was shown into a large room,' he said…"

"He" here could refer to Milnes (the subject of the prior sentence) or to Adams (the broader subject of the paragraph). The source makes clear this is Milnes's anecdote — he is the speaker of the quoted dialogue. In the draft, "he said" appears as an attribution of the dialogue, but the preceding sentence's "he" (referring to Milnes, who "was almost as helpless") is the same "he" who then "bubbled with delight" and is then the speaker of "I was shown into a large room." So Milnes is the antecedent.

Actually, reading the draft paragraph more carefully: "Even Milnes, who felt the splendors of Hugo and Landor, was almost as helpless in personal contact with them. Ten years afterwards he bubbled with delight at a call on Hugo: 'I was shown into a large room,' he said…" — "he" refers to Milnes, which is the correct reading and matches the source. A competent reader follows Milnes as the subject without confusion. Not a finding.

**Ch 011 draft — "The three young men returned to London"**

Source: "The three young men returned to London, and each went his own way."

Draft: "The three young men returned to London, and each went his own way."

Wait — who are "the three young men"? In the source, the party at Fryston consists of five: Milnes, Stirling, Oliphant, Swinburne, and Adams. The source explains this as "the five" or "the party of five men." The source's "three young men" refers to Swinburne, Oliphant, and Adams (leaving out Milnes and Stirling as older). In the draft, the Fryston party is described as "Of the four besides Adams" — four guests plus Adams = five people. The draft has not clarified who "the three young men" are. A reader might be confused about which three of the five are meant.

Let me check the source more carefully: "The three young men returned to London" — in the source this follows a long section on Swinburne, Oliphant, and Adams. Stirling and Milnes are implicitly not "young men." In the draft, Stirling is described as "a quiet, agreeable gentleman of the literary class" (no age marker), Oliphant as "a grave and charming younger man," Swinburne as "a boy in look though older than Adams." So in the draft, three of the four guests (Oliphant, Swinburne, Adams plus…?) could be "young men." Milnes is called "the oldest" in the draft. Stirling's age is not specified.

Actually the source says Stirling was "of a certain age" — an older man. So the three young men = Oliphant, Swinburne, Adams. In the draft, this grouping is derivable by inference (Milnes is oldest; Stirling is "of a certain age" in source but that's cut). In the draft Stirling's age is not marked. A reader might wonder why Stirling isn't among the three returning to London. This is borderline — but I think the gate test passes because a reader would simply understand "three young men" as the younger members of the party without being genuinely confused about the plot.

Not a finding.

**Ch 011 draft — "Of Swinburne he saw no more save once at a great dinner, famous then but no nearer."**

Source: "Of Swinburne he saw no more till Monckton Milnes summoned his whole array of Frystonians to support him in presiding at the dinner of the Authors' Fund, when Adams found himself seated next to Swinburne, famous then, but no nearer. They never met again."

Draft: "Of Swinburne he saw no more save once at a great dinner, famous then but no nearer."

"Famous then but no nearer" — in the source "famous then, but no nearer" means Swinburne was now famous (after Poems and Ballads) but no nearer (in personal terms) to Adams. In the draft this reads naturally the same way. Not a structural break.

---

**Ch 011 draft — closing summary paragraphs**

The final two paragraphs ("Yet for all this, the education of 1862…" and "If a year's schooling was meant to teach…") are a compression-summary not present in the source. These are additions by the drafter, not compressions. No structural damage to test.

---

**Ch 010 draft — "By way of teaching him quickly, the Government sent out the new Minister to Russia, Cassius M. Clay, in the same ship—a teacher having no equal though possibly some rivals."**

Source: "By way of teaching him quickly, they sent out their new Minister to Russia in the same ship. Secretary Seward had occasion to learn the merits of Cassius M. Clay in the diplomatic service, but Mr. Seward's education profited less than the private secretary's, Cassius Clay as a teacher having no equal though possibly some rivals."

Draft: "By way of teaching him quickly, the Government sent out the new Minister to Russia, Cassius M. Clay, in the same ship—a teacher having no equal though possibly some rivals."

The source explains that Clay was a teacher of the private secretary (Seward's education profited less than the private secretary's). The draft phrases it as "a teacher having no equal" — the referent of "a teacher" is Clay, described immediately before. But the point — that Clay taught the private secretary — is preserved by implication. A reader understands Clay was an instructive (if alarming) shipmate. Not a structural break.

---

**Ch 010 draft — "The private secretary could not grumble to his chief."**

Source: "No young man, not in Government pay, could be asked to draw, from such lessons, any confidence in himself… Above all, the private secretary could not grumble to his chief."

Draft: The paragraph about Cassius Clay ends with "—a teacher having no equal though possibly some rivals." The very next sentence is "The private secretary could not grumble to his chief."

In the source there is an intervening passage about young men in government pay drawing no confidence. In the draft that is cut, and we jump to "The private secretary could not grumble to his chief." Does this constitute a broken pivot? The "above all" connective in the source is gone. In the draft there's no connective — it just moves on. A competent reader reads this as a new observation about the private secretary's situation. Not a broken pivot because there's no false connective; it just lacks the "above all" escalator. Not a finding.

---

**Ch 010 draft — "But for the Minister, on the spot, the danger was not so imminent."**

Source: "Politically the prospect looked even worse, and for Secretary Seward and Senator Sumner it was so; but for the Minister, on the spot, as he came to realize exactly where he stood, the danger was not so imminent."

Draft: "Politically and socially, the outlook was desperate. A newcomer in London society needs years to establish a position, and Minister Adams had not a week to spare. But for the Minister, on the spot, the danger was not so imminent."

The "but" contrasts with the preceding point that the outlook was desperate / Adams had not a week to spare. In the source the "but" contrasts with "for Secretary Seward and Senator Sumner it was so" — meaning the danger WAS imminent for Seward/Sumner but not for the Minister. In the draft, the Seward/Sumner arm of the contrast is cut. The "but" now contrasts with "Minister Adams had not a week to spare," which is a reasonable contrast (time was short — but the actual danger was less immediate). A competent reader can follow this. Not a genuine structural break.

---

**Ch 010 draft — "The singular luck that took him to Fryston to meet the shock of the Trent Affair under the sympathetic eyes of Monckton Milnes and William E. Forster never afterwards deserted him."**

This references "Fryston" — is this established in the draft? Yes: earlier in the draft, "They telegraphed the news to the Minister, who was staying with Monckton Milnes at Fryston in Yorkshire." So Fryston is established in the preceding draft chapter. Not a mid-scene jump.

**Ch 011 draft — "Just as Brunnow predicted, Lord Palmerston made his rush at last, as unexpected as always, and more furiously than though still a private secretary of twenty-four."**

Source has this identical sentence. "Just as Brunnow predicted" — was Brunnow's prediction mentioned in the draft? In the draft's Cambridge House paragraph: "In the case of Palmerston they were unanimous in warning new colleagues that they might expect to be sacrificed by him to any momentary personal object." Brunnow is named only in the "C'est une peau de rhinocere!" quotation: "not even the Queen—for, as old Baron Brunnow described him: 'C'est une peau de rhinocere!'" So Brunnow appears in the draft but as the author of a description, not explicitly as the one who predicted Palmerston's "rush." The source does not have an explicit Brunnow prediction scene either — it just says "as Brunnow predicted" referencing something general. A reader understands this as a nod to a diplomat's general warning. Not a genuine structural break requiring source knowledge.

**Ch 011 draft — "Lady Palmerston tried her best, but the two ladies found no resource except tears."**

Source: "Lady Palmerston tried her best, but the two ladies found no resource except tears. They had to do with American Minister perplexed in the extreme."

Draft: "Lady Palmerston tried her best, but the two ladies found no resource except tears."

"The two ladies" — who is the second lady? In the source context this is Lady Palmerston and Lady Jocelyn (mentioned in the Cambridge House routine passage in the source). In the draft, Lady Jocelyn is never mentioned. Lady Palmerston is named. Who is the second lady? A competent reader has no way to know from the draft.

Let me check: in the draft's Cambridge House section, the only woman named is Lady Palmerston. "Lady Jocelyn with her daughter" appears in the source's Saturday-evening routine passage but is not in the draft. So "the two ladies" has only one identifiable antecedent (Lady Palmerston) in the draft. This is a genuine dangling reference — the second lady is unidentifiable from the draft alone.

**This is a valid finding.**

---

**Ch 011 draft — "Of Swinburne he saw no more save once at a great dinner, famous then but no nearer. Oliphant all the world knew and loved, and then he, too, disappeared."**

"he, too, disappeared" — "he" refers to Oliphant. The "too" implies another person also disappeared. In the source: "They never met again. Oliphant he met oftener; all the world knew and loved him; but he too disappeared in the way that all the world knows. Stirling of Keir, after one or two efforts, passed also from Adams's vision…" — so the "too" in source means Oliphant disappeared as Swinburne (became more remote). In the draft: "Of Swinburne he saw no more save once at a great dinner, famous then but no nearer. Oliphant all the world knew and loved, and then he, too, disappeared." The "too" implies Oliphant disappeared like Swinburne — that's clear enough. A reader can follow this. Not a finding.

---

**Ch 010 draft — "He thought on May 12 that he was going to a friendly Government and people…"**

This paragraph has no explicit subject introduction — "He thought on May 12…" — who is "he"? The preceding paragraph ends: "Though Palmerston would have laughed at figuring as Tiberius, he had already arranged the ceremony." So "he" could refer to Palmerston or Henry Adams. The source makes clear this is Henry Adams's thought. In the draft, the preceding paragraph's last clause has "he" = Palmerston. Then "He thought on May 12 that he was going to a friendly Government" — a reader would naturally take this as Adams (the consistent subject throughout), not Palmerston. The broader context of the draft (Henry's education, his thoughts) makes this parseable. Not a genuine confusion.

---

**Ch 011 draft — "As education this first country visit had value. Milnes mixed strange elements. The winter mists of Yorkshire hung heavy; the hostess was absent; the guests had nothing to do but astonish each other."**

In source: "Fryston was one of a class of houses that no one sought for its natural beauties, and the winter mists of Yorkshire were rather more evident for the absence of the hostess on account of them." The source connects the hostess's absence to the winter mists — she was away because of the weather. The draft severs this: "The winter mists of Yorkshire hung heavy; the hostess was absent" makes them coincident but doesn't say the mists caused the absence. A reader simply reads two independent atmospheric facts. Not a structural break that misleads.

---

**Ch 011 draft — "smoking being forbidden in 1862 even when ladies were not in the house, Milnes gave his guests Adams's bedroom"**

Source: "in 1862, even when ladies were not in the house, smoking was forbidden, and guests usually smoked in the stables or the kitchen; but Monckton Milnes was a licensed libertine who let his guests smoke in Adams's bedroom, since Adams was an American-German barbarian ignorant of manners"

Draft: "smoking being forbidden in 1862 even when ladies were not in the house, Milnes gave his guests Adams's bedroom" — the "since Adams was an American-German barbarian ignorant of manners" explanation is cut. The draft just says Milnes gave them Adams's bedroom. A reader wonders why Adams's room specifically but is not genuinely misled. Not a structural break.
